summary:
Emergency Ordinance No. 89/2001, adopted 21 June 2001 and in force 26 June 2001, repealed Penal Code Article 200 and decriminalised consensual adult same-sex relations; Articles 197, 198, 201 and 202 were redefined in gender-neutral terms applying equally to sexual acts with persons of different or same sex. Pending investigations, trials and custodial sentences under former Article 200(2)–(4) were preserved only where the facts remained punishable under other provisions, with reclassification by the execution court. Same-sex relations are legal nationwide.

Legal gender recognition is possible in Romania and has been since 1996 for a person who has undergone sex reassignment surgery, but the governing law is vague and incomplete and judicial practice is inconsistent: some authorities refuse recognition unless a surgical intervention occurred. A change of civil status requires a court decision that in practice rests on a certificate from the Institutul Național de Medicină Legală, issued through an intrusive and arbitrary procedure developed ad hoc to fill a legal vacuum. The difficulty of that procedure frequently prevents identity documents from reflecting a person's gender identity, which in turn produces documented problems in health care, transport passes and banking services. ILGA-Europe's assessment for January to December 2025 records that legal gender recognition still has no fair, transparent, self-determination-based framework free from abusive requirements, and no non-binary option.

The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in October 2024, in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, that Romania had infringed a transgender man's rights; the case concerns recognition in Romania of a UK gender recognition certificate. On 31 March 2026 the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates. The judgment builds on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe legal gender recognition carried out in another EU country; ACCEPT Romania announced it on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

Statutory protection does not name transgender people. Stated anti-discrimination, hate-crime aggravation and incitement provisions are framed on the basis of sexual orientation, and hate crime and hate speech protections lack express coverage of gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics. Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, and a 2000 law extends that prohibition across employment, goods and services, housing, education, health care, audiovisual programming, justice, public services and social security, enforced by the National Council for Combating Discrimination; Outright International's overview of 12 March 2026 records that institutional follow-through on that framework is limited.

Official rhetoric during 2025 targeted gender markers directly. In the presidential campaign, candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February 2025 and Prime Minister Marcel Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review records Ciolacu as opposing amendments to identity documents to accommodate legal gender recognition on the ground that they create confusion and erode traditional norms. In October 2025 political figures claimed that children could choose their gender without parental consent, in response to recommendations in the European Commission's LGBTI Equality Strategy 2026-2030.

The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August 2025 after the channel's News Pass programme of 5 June 2025 framed Pride as a provocation and used derogatory portrayals of LGBTI visibility. The warning cited breach of the Audiovisual Code prohibition on generalised defamatory statements against groups defined by sexual orientation, following a complaint by ACCEPT.

Pride events proceeded under visible strain. The Bucharest Pride march of 7 June 2025 drew approximately 31,000 people, who demanded simplified legal gender recognition procedures, civil union legislation and protection against hate speech and prejudice-based crimes; AP reported on the 20th anniversary of the march in June 2025, with tens of thousands marching amid rising right-wing hostility. In July 2025 Oradea Pride went ahead despite a third-year attempt by the municipality to ban it, under heavy police supervision, with nine organisers and participants fined and a subsequent application to the European Court of Human Rights; Pride events in Cluj-Napoca, Brașov, Timișoara and Iași took place without incidents.

Three training-of-trainers sessions for police officers, prosecutors and social workers were held in October 2025 on recognising, investigating and responding to hate crimes targeting LGBTI people.

There is no marriage or civil union recognition. Marriage is limited to a union between a man and a woman under Civil Code Article 259 and its implementing legislation; the 2018 constitutional-ban referendum failed on low turnout, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017. The European Court of Human Rights ruled on 23 May 2023 that a failure to allow marriage or partnership breaches Article 8, and the Prime Minister said in November 2023 that Romania will not legalise either. For a trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex, the Court of Justice ruled in Coman in June 2018 that same-sex spouses married in an EU country have residence rights, and Romania's highest courts granted the same residency and legal rights in 2018.

Legislative attempts to restrict discussion of gender identity have been blocked. A June 2020 parliament amendment imposing a blanket ban on gender identity studies without public debate was struck down by the Constitutional Court in December 2020. In April 2022 the Senate passed bills banning 'gay propaganda' in schools and banning discussion of homosexuality and gender identity in public spaces; the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the final version.
tangentialFactors:
Romania's election period is cited in the ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion among the country chapters: of nine submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people. The Romania chapter was authored by ACCEPT Romania.

The Council of Europe published a national thematic review in January 2023, 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania', covering the legal and policy framework, applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law and international standards for implementing Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5.

A FRA-commissioned legal study of February 2008 by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners, including national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints. It is a dated baseline for the protection architecture rather than a current assessment.

Public opinion data in the inventory measures LGBT populations broadly and is not trans-specific. The IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition. A 2019 poll of approximately 3,200 people found 53% of LGBTI respondents were '(Almost) never open' about being LGBTI, 23% rarely open, 18% fairly open and 7% very open. The inventory contains no separate transgender-specific tolerance figure beyond the general statement that attitudes in Romania are conservative regarding the rights of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender citizens.

Men who have sex with men remain barred from blood donation under a rule found to be illegal sexual-orientation discrimination in September 2007; a January 2008 Health Ministry removal of the ban is recorded as not yet implemented. The rule is framed on sexual conduct rather than gender identity.

The CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials during 2023. In March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew protests from 13 religious groups and a counter-response from a 50-plus organisation.

Open LGBT visibility remains concentrated in major urban centres, with annual pride parades in Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Iași and Timișoara; the 18th Bucharest Pride drew 25,000 participants. The 7 June 2025 march drew approximately 31,000. Raw participation counts are not a per-capita risk measure.
localsOnly:
Changing civil status requires a court decision supported by a certificate from the Institutul Național de Medicină Legală, obtained through a procedure developed ad hoc outside a clear statutory framework. Since 1996 the route has been available to a person who has undergone sex reassignment surgery, and authorities in some cases deny recognition where no surgical intervention occurred. The resulting gap between legal status and documents is documented as producing difficulties in health care, transport passes and banking services.

Discrimination complaints on grounds of sex or sexual orientation go to the National Council for Combating Discrimination under Government Ordinance 137/2000 and the 2000 law covering employment, goods and services, housing, education, health care, audiovisual programming, justice, public services and social security. The CNCD has used those powers, including a fine against TAROM for refusing same-sex partners couples discounts in 2005 and the 2023 investigation of printing houses that refused LGBT and gender-equality material. Outright International's March 2026 overview records institutional follow-through as limited.

The Penal Code was amended in 2006 to add incitement to discrimination, homophobic bias as an aggravating circumstance permitting higher sentences, and incitement to hatred and harassment on sexual-orientation grounds; the inventory describes application of those provisions as difficult to assess or not yet applied, and none of them names gender identity.

Residents seeking to organise face municipal resistance: Oradea's municipality attempted a ban on the city's Pride for a third consecutive year in July 2025, and nine organisers and participants were fined before an application was taken to the European Court of Human Rights. LGBTI organisations can register in Romania, and a civil-partnership bill has been pending since 2017 with the Orthodox Church opposed to it.

Education policy has been a recurring site of restriction: a June 2020 amendment banning gender identity studies without public debate was struck down by the Constitutional Court in December 2020, and the anti-LGBTQ provisions of the April 2022 Senate bills on 'gay propaganda' and public discussion of homosexuality and gender identity were removed in the final version.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory gives conflicting dates for Emergency Ordinance No. 89/2001: the primary legal text records adoption on 21 June 2001 and entry into force on 26 June 2001, while a secondary reference dates adoption to January 2001 and effect to January 2002 after presidential signature. The discrepancy is unresolved here; the substance of decriminalisation is not in dispute.

No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border procedures, airport or checkpoint screening, document-marker flagging at the border, or treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers by border or security staff. Nothing should be inferred either way from their absence.

No current trans-specific violence prevalence figure with a denominator is sourced for Romania. The survey evidence available measures LGBT populations broadly, is framed around sexual orientation, or closed years ago, so no trans-specific rate can be stated.

Whether the 2006 Penal Code aggravating circumstance and incitement provisions have been applied in any documented case is described in the source as difficult to assess or not yet applied; no case-level outcome is sourced. The status of the January 2008 Health Ministry removal of the men-who-have-sex-with-men blood donation ban is recorded as not implemented, with no later confirmation in the inventory.

Whether the CJEU's 2024 transcription ruling has produced further birth-certificate orders beyond the Mirzarafie-Ahi judgment of 31 March 2026 is not sourced; ACCEPT Romania's public invitation to others suggests the route is open but the inventory documents one case.
